name: PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: London Sumatra — an estate the market barely pays for
frontmatter.summary: A mature planter whose cash is most of its market value and whose estate the market barely pays for. We stay BUY at Rp4,668 (205.4%) after answering the red team: upstream-only peer marks, a sourced maturity ramp in the base, the related-party cash moved to unrelated banks and a mirrored cost shock. GAPKI's national El Nino warning changes no base input [S24, S25].
thesis: Cash of IDR8,516.3bn and no interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 is most of the IDR10,639.1bn market capitalisation [S8, F37].
A mature estate earned 43.5% EBITDA margins at the deck price, with most output sold domestically to the parent at a persistent discount to the export benchmark [S7, S15].
The dividend is covered at a thirty per cent payout and a IDR750.0bn buyback is running; a probability-weighted part of the buyback is in the target and the dividend step-up is not [S12, S9].
The DCF, the config-blend multiples and book value all sit far above the price; the reverse DCF implies CPO near US$647/t [S0].
The risk is structural: related-party offtake, a controlling holder with no obligation to distribute, and a payout already cut once [S7, S12, S13].

catalysts.event: Implementing finance-ministry regulation for the DHE SDA conversion amendment; no direct effect on LSIP, watched only for the exchange-rate channel

blocks.text: **Update, 13 November 2026 — the El Nino warning, the DSI tariff and the red team's round.** GAPKI's chairman said El Nino could cost Indonesian palm output up to 3m tonnes in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68, S22], but the warning gives no regional or company breakdown, the company gives no 2027 guidance, and the nine months to September precede that harvest [S24, S3, S8], so no national percentage enters a company plan. Volume instead carries the one sourced driver, the 84,744 ha of immature oil palm maturing, taking the plan from 300 kt to 315 kt [S6, F40]. The DSI single export channel starts 1 January 2027 with the tariff due in December [S20, S25]; London Sumatra's IDR43.7bn export line is rubber, cocoa and tea [S7, F49], so the regime reaches it only through the parent's refining netback, carried in the bear [S21].

At Rp1,560 the company is worth about IDR10,639.1bn against IDR8,516.3bn of cash and no interest-bearing debt [S8]. Nine-month profit rose two fifths but not on the estate: other operating income rose to IDR290.8bn from IDR99.8bn on land receipts and FX gains and the bio-asset line swung to a gain [S8], so underlying operating profit grew about a fifth. Our target is Rp4,668, 205.4% above the price: a DCF at the through-cycle deck plus cash with a governance discount. This revision changed four inputs, not the peer marks: the thirteen pure planters (about four per cent off), the maturity ramp in the base volume (about two per cent on), a thirty-five per cent trapped-cash probability [F78], and a mirrored bull cost relief — a net target about one and a half per cent below the published one. The reverse DCF is the discipline: the price implies US$647/t against a deck of 1,240.0 USD/t [S0, S15].

PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk has nucleus estates in North Sumatra, South Sumatra, East Kalimantan, Java and Sulawesi [S6]. It sold 290.0 kt CPO of CPO from just over one hundred and ten thousand planted hectares — about ninety-one thousand oil palm, sixteen thousand rubber and the balance cocoa and tea [S6]. This is an upstream grower and miller: no refining of consequence, and the economics are the CPO price less the cost of a tonne [S7].

More than three fifths of revenue goes to PT Salim Ivomas Pratama, the listed subsidiary of Indofood Agri that controls London Sumatra [S7]. Sales are market-referenced, and the audited realisation was stable in rupiah against the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB [S7, F41]. Strategy is replanting, yield recovery and cost control: planted area has drifted down over five years, with no announced expansion or downstream project [S6].

The Salim family controls the company: Salim Ivomas holds 59.5% and Indofood Agri a further small stake, the group just under three fifths, the public 40.4% [S13]. All 6,820 m shares are listed; no special-monitoring-board designation or notation letter appears in the filings we hold [S7, S8].

Indonesia is the world's largest CPO producer, and the price London Sumatra receives is set globally. The deck has CPO averaging 1,135.0 USD/t this year, rising next year and easing toward 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with Indonesian inflation [S0, S15].

On 12 November GAPKI put a number on the weather: up to 3m tonnes, heaviest in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68, S22]. Against a national crop of about sixty million tonnes that is a loss in the region of a twentieth; London Sumatra's 300 kt is under one per cent of it. GAPKI gives no regional or company breakdown and neither the company nor its filings give 2027 guidance [S24, S3, S8], so the company-level yield risk is the bear, at a shortfall of about a sixth; the investment-risks section sizes five and ten per cent. The nine-month recovery is evidence about 2026, not the 2027 harvest [S3]. Against the supply loss stands the B50 mandate, needing 14m tonnes a year [S22] — a price channel, not an LSIP volume channel, and the bull's case. We make no claim that the house deck prices the weather: it is a CPO series with no weather variable, used at its published levels [S0].

Policy is active. CPO exports carry a levy plus duty that moves monthly; for November the combined charge fell by a fifth to 246.4 USD/t per tonne, borne by the exporter and marginal here because sales are domestic [S10]. From 1 January 2027 coal, CPO and ferro alloy would file through DSI's portal, reported but unconfirmed [S20]; the palm tariff is not yet set, to be announced in December at a working estimate in the single-digit dollar range [S25], so the incidence is indirect through the parent's export netback, and the bear carries a sized pass-through [S21]. The exchange-control change is separate and negligible here: PP 21/2026 brings DHE SDA onshore, but palm and seed revenue is rupiah from a domestic customer [S17, S7].

No domestic levy is in force in November 2026 [S10]; B50's funding need is the one route to a charge on domestic sales, priced at thirty to sixty dollars per tonne in the bear. London Sumatra's estates are old, and its cash cost of 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne rose because external FFB purchases climbed by more than a third [S7, S6]. The moat is land and logistics — HGU rights, mills, plasma partnerships, the parent's refining system — barriers that do not protect margins from a falling price [S6]. Five forces: unfavourable on the customer side, neutral on suppliers, favourable against new entrants [S6].

The data pack misstates the last audited year. Revenue rose 20.8% to IDR5,511.7bn on higher CPO volume and price; operating profit was IDR2,008.4bn and net profit to the parent IDR1,887.8bn [S7]. The pack's depreciation is unusable — a few billion against audited IDR389.5bn — so we key the audited figure, lift FY2025 EBITDA to IDR2,397.8bn and margin to 43.5%, restate FY2024 the same way, and strike multiples off this base [S7, F12].

The cash cost is 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne, backed out of audited cost of sales after removing depreciation and allocating other costs; it rose on external FFB purchases, and we hold it in real terms with inflation [S7]. Realisation is calibrated on the nine-month interim: CPO revenue over CPO volume gives a dollar price flat against prior year while the benchmark rose, ratio 75.8% [S8, S3, S0]. Audited 858.1 USD/t against 1,007.0 USD/t is not like-for-like, because the World Bank replaced its palm-oil series in January 2026 [S15, S0]; LSIP invoices against the domestic Harga Referensi, averaging 14,234 rupiah per kilogram [S10, F41].

Revenue rises to IDR5,988.9bn this year, EBITDA IDR2,684.3bn, net profit IDR2,189.5bn and Rp321 per share. Volume is 300 kt this year, the nine-month run-rate plus a normal fourth quarter, then 305 kt, 310 kt and 315 kt as the immature block enters production: 84,744 mature hectares of 110,982 planted, an oil palm three to four years from planting to harvest, and mature area drifting down over five years, so the path is the net of maturation and attrition [S6, F32, F40]. It is below the gross arithmetic and about a twelfth above FY2025 sales [F1]. The model's dollar ASP of 860.3 USD/t at the current-year benchmark is flat against last year's realised 858.1 USD/t [S8, S3, S15].

FY2026E reconciles to the interim. The fourth quarter is a normal quarter, not the nine-month run-rate: revenue is IDR5,988.9bn against IDR4,326.7bn for the nine months, and net profit IDR2,189.5bn against IDR1,743.8bn. The gap is two non-recurring credits: other operating income rose to IDR290.8bn from IDR99.8bn — land-usage receipts IDR157.0bn against IDR38.3bn, net FX gains IDR125.9bn against IDR51.5bn — and the bio-asset line swung from a IDR32.5bn loss to a IDR72.2bn gain [S8, note 23]. Neither recurs at that level: strip both and nine-month operating profit grew about a fifth. Opex is therefore held at the audited 4.6% of revenue, the lowest of the four audited years, not a cautious anchor; on the interim's recurring lines alone the ratio is half again as high and the target about three per cent lower [S7, S8, F35, F74, F75, F76].

Capex runs at 7.9% of revenue, the top of its four-year range, and working capital is small; EBITDA becomes cash [S7]: IDR8,516.3bn at the third quarter against zero interest-bearing debt [S8]. The annual report discloses no tree-age profile, replanting schedule or five-year capex average — the immature series is the only age evidence — so we test a steady-state replanting rate of about a tenth of revenue: it takes about five per cent off the target and leaves the rating unchanged [S6, F40]. Working capital is held at the FY2025 ratio and the bear stretches it to the FY2024 spike; capex escalates with inflation [S0, F34]. Dividend Rp83 at thirty per cent payout [S12]. Operating cash flow of IDR3,015.7bn exceeded net profit and the accruals ratio is negative three years [S7, S0]; inventories of IDR830.8bn are a build of a third that one quarter explains but a second would not [S8, S3].

We use a DCF as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks at sixty, twenty-five and fifteen per cent — the set for a price-taking grower. Terminal growth is 2.5%, long-run rupiah inflation [S0].

The cost of equity is 11.2%: the rupiah ten-year yield 7.4% [S18] less the 1.6% sovereign default spread, plus beta 0.80 times the mature premium 4.2% and country premium 2.5% [S19]. The deduction is not a discount to the hurdle: the ten-year yield already carries sovereign risk, so it is removed before the country premium is added back scaled by beta. Beta is the PLANTATIONS config default, not a measured regression, and the assumptions say so [S0]. At a thirteen per cent cost of equity the target is about a tenth lower, at fifteen per cent about a sixth lower, and even then about two and a half times the price. With no net debt WACC equals the cost of equity.

The DCF gives Rp5,163 per share, a terminal value of 46.0% of it, on an enterprise value of IDR25,462.5bn plus September net cash and the associate. The anchor is the deck's through-cycle 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with inflation, so the first terminal year is 1,178.8 USD/t, not the 1,180.0 USD/t print [S0, S15]. We use the deck's shape, not a cross-series level: the World Bank replaced its palm-oil series in January 2026 [S15 p.3], so pre-2026 averages are not homogeneous. On the new series the anchor is about two and a half per cent below spot and about one and a third per cent above the 1,135.0 USD/t deck average.

The IDR1,261.1bn associate line is four equity-method holdings — Asian Assets Management in Singapore and PT Aston Inti Makmur in Jakarta, each roughly a quarter held, plus two smaller industrial-timber holdings [S7, S8, F62]. Both larger are private and carried below attributable net assets; the nine-month share of profit was IDR1.5bn, a negligible return on book [S8, F67]. At attributable net assets they would be worth about a fortieth of the target more, disclosed and not added. Cash at face plus the associate at book means the market pays about a third of last year's EBITDA for the estate, just over two fifths after the related-party haircut.

The cross-checks are struck on the thirteen pure upstream planters, not the industry-wide pack set whose median carried downstream refiners and holding companies at several times a grower's multiple [S0]: the EV/EBITDA median 5.1x gives Rp3,228 and the P/BV blend 0.9x gives Rp1,967, below the DCF by about two fifths and three fifths. The EV/EBITDA leg uses the trailing restated FY2025A EBITDA, not IDR2,684.3bn of FY2026E; on the forward figure the target would be about one per cent higher, weights unchanged. The gap is a terminal-value effect: EV is operating FCFF only, cash and the associate added in the equity bridge, so the multiple holds no deposit yield.

The group anchors are the harder test and sit outside the median. SIMP, the parent that sets the offtake, trades at a lower EV/EBITDA and a fraction of book than LSIP, and AALI, the sister, at a middle multiple and about three quarters of book [model.peers]. At the parent's EV/EBITDA LSIP would be worth about half our target and one and a half times the price; at the parent's book multiple, about half the price. That is why the DCF carries sixty per cent: a minority in a controlled subsidiary does not receive a mark the parent's own minority does not, and the parent's discount is the governance discount we charge in the bridge.

The bridge has three items. The trapped-cash discount is charged only to the related-party cash at PT Bank Ina Perdana, IDR665.0bn at 30 September, 4.0% of assets and under a tenth of cash [S8, F53, F54]; in the persistence state it is worth about two fifths of face, so at thirty-five per cent the charge is about a fifth of that slice — the step down from even odds is worth under a per cent of the target. The interim argues for the lower probability: the balance fell from IDR1,639.6bn at the prior year-end and moved onto the company's own balance sheet at unrelated banks — third-party time deposits up from IDR5,658.9bn to IDR7,629.3bn, led by IDR3,078.5bn at Danamon — while total cash rose [S8, F39, F53, F78, F79, F80, F57]. The payout cut and the absence of a minority veto keep the probability from zero. The IDR750.0bn buyback to 31 December 2026 [S9] is counted at half size and even odds; the third item is a related-party deployment charge at a quarter probability, sized in the investment-risks section [S7, S13]. The rest of the deposits is at face: the haircut is not a credit loss but cash permanently undistributable to minorities [S8, F57].
The rest of the deposits is at face: the haircut is not a credit loss [S8, F57].

Two caveats on the grids: they are struck from the base scenario before the probabilities, so even the clean grid's centre prints at Rp4,573, not the published Rp4,668; and the benchmark override holds the benchmark at its last explicit level, so a multiplier of one changes nothing until FY2031E, costing about a fourteenth of the base target and about a tenth of the DCF.

The reverse DCF is a DCF statement and reconciles with the grid: the grid prints the blended twelve-month target, whose multiple legs are struck on trailing marks and do not move with CPO, while the reverse DCF solves the DCF leg alone. At a clean four fifths of the deck the DCF alone is about double the price, and at half the deck about a tenth below; the price is reached just over half the deck up, exactly the reverse-DCF answer of US$647/t against 1,240.0 USD/t [S0, S15]. We judge this fourth path one chance in ten — two years of flat dollar realisation and a persistent discount is what a market expecting sub-cycle prices looks like [S8, S3] — and weighting it so would put the target about seven per cent below the published one, a rating that survives.

The largest risk is that the discount is permanent. London Sumatra is a controlled subsidiary of a family group, most output is sold to its parent, and a material share of cash sat with a related bank — IDR665.0bn at 30 September, 4.0% of total assets, withdrawable at the group's discretion [S8, F53]. The interim shows the balance moving to unrelated banks [S8], which cuts the probability but not the premise: minorities cannot force a distribution and the payout has been cut once. We charge for it: a quarter probability on a value-destroying related-party deployment before FY2028 — two trillion rupiah at twice fair value destroys one trillion, a thirty-odd rupiah per share, under one per cent of the target — on top of the trapped-cash discount, resting on the related-party share of revenue and the absence of a minority veto [S7, F34, S13].

The second risk is CPO. The base uses the house deck at its published levels; if the weather premium fades and Malaysian stocks rebuild, price could fall by a quarter or more [S11], the bear's price shock. The GAPKI warning cuts both ways: a 3m tonne loss meeting a B50 mandate that needs 14m tonnes is the bull's price case, while the same loss on London Sumatra's own estates is the bear's volume case [S24, S22]; the first-half 2027 production report is the test [S24]. A five per cent company-level shortfall takes roughly a twentieth off EBITDA and a ten per cent shortfall roughly a tenth, but only about two and four per cent off the target because cash and the associate carry most of the value.

The third cluster is operational and regulatory. Deferred fertiliser is a cost risk [S22]; the levy and biodiesel mandate change the domestic price [S10]; from January the reported single-channel export regime adds an unpublished intermediary cost between the group's refineries and the world market [S20, S21]. A one-to-five per cent pass-through into the related-party offtake, 63.3% of revenue, is about one and a half to eight per cent of EBITDA and moves the target one to four per cent, carried in the bear. A domestic levy at thirty to sixty dollars per tonne, capitalised, is five to nine per cent of the target; the bear carries forty dollars. FY2024's IDR296.2bn rubber impairment could recur [S7]. Turnover of IDR17.8bn and a 40.4% public float clear the fund's floor, so no liquidity discount applies [S0, S13, F60].

The scenarios mirror the base shock for shock: the bear holds CPO at seventy-one and a half per cent of the deck at the reference year [S15], volume down about a sixth, the real cost base three tenths higher (including the levy and the single-channel pass-through) and working capital stretched; the bull raises price by two fifths, volume about a sixth, releases working capital and holds costs at the reciprocal relief, about a quarter below the last actual. The bear charges the related-party cash discount at the even-odds reading, so it is an operating bear, and it still produces Rp2,414, above the price: even at the cycle's realised low the market pays less than the estate alone is worth. The probability-weighted target is Rp4,668. Signposts: a sustained CPO break below the bear, a 2027 harvest where London Sumatra's own output falls with the national crop while price does not rise [S24], a related-party transfer of cash out below market value, a further deposit shift away from the group bank or back to it, another payout cut, a levy materially above forty dollars, or the buyback abandoned.

The controlling shareholder is PT Salim Ivomas Pratama of the Indofood Agri group, holding 59.5%, with Indofood Agri a further stake; the group controls just under three fifths and the public 40.4% of the 6,820 m shares [S13]. We use the company's table, not the Yahoo insider field of seventy per cent, which is impossible and unused [S0, S13]. We find no pledge disclosure, control contest or restatement; the board has group nominees and independent commissioners [S7, S8]. Related-party dealings are the central governance fact: sales of more than three fifths of revenue to the parent, FFB purchases from related estates, finance income on deposits at a related bank and group service companies all appear in the notes [S7]. Each is disclosed at market-referenced terms; the audited realisation discount was stable across the two audited years [S7, S15]. The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with an unmodified opinion [S7]; the company does not revalue plantations, so P/BV is a floor. The dividend record is the counterweight: a payout every year, thirty per cent for the last two years and thirty-five before [S12]; the cut is why the trap probability stays above zero.

On ESG the exposures are land and deforestation, peat, labour and smallholder relations; the estates are long established, the company operates plasma partnerships and reports against the national sustainability standard [S6].

The near-term catalyst is the full-year result and the dividend declaration that follows; the interim showed underlying operating profit up about a fifth and cash higher, so the base for the final dividend is strong [S3, S8, F71, F77]. The buyback runs to 31 December 2026 on internal cash [S9], accretive at the current price.

Policy is the third catalyst: the B50 mandate and monthly export levy reset determine the domestic CPO price and the group's offtake economics [S10], and a domestic levy is the risk we watch. On 1 January the reported DSI portal is due to open for CPO and coal; we watch the December tariff announcement [S25] and whether the group's export netback moves [S20, S21].

The operational signposts are FFB output, extraction rate and external FFB purchases; nine months showed recovery on all three [S3]. GAPKI dates the heaviest El Nino impact to the 2027 harvest [S24, F68], so the first-half production report is where the warning shows up in London Sumatra's own yields or does not. Above all we monitor related-party flows: a change in the offtake, the deposit relationship or the group's willingness to let cash accumulate matters more than the CPO price [S7, S13].

bear.narrative: The discount persists and the cycle troughs at the same time. The related-party cash slice at Bank Ina Perdana of Rp665.016bn at 30-Sep-2026 is not withdrawn and the whole-balance governance failure is quoted as a separate state in section 5 [S8, F53]. On top of that, CPO is held at 71.5% of the new-series deck for the whole forecast, close to 29% below the deck own floor and stated only as a percentage of the current deck: the pre-2026 World Bank levels and averages are not comparable after the January-2026 series replacement [S15, p.3], so no cross-series level is used anywhere in this paper. The El Nino premium unwinds and Malaysian stocks rebuild [S11], a weaker FFB crop cuts volume 15% from the 300 kt plan - the GAPKI 3m tonne national loss [S24, F68] made company-specific, with a second season of fertiliser deferred on cost [S22] - and the parent receivable stretches working capital twofold from the FY2025 3.3% of revenue, which is the widest shock the engine bounds allow; the FY2024 actual stretch to 21.7% is disclosed in sections 3 and 5 as a stress beyond the kept scenario set, so the one year that actually stretched is representable even though the multiplier cannot reach it [S0, F34]. The cost stress is 30% above the FY2025 real level: 20% from external FFB and fertiliser, plus a USD40/t domestic CPO levy and a 2% pass-through of the DSI single-channel fee into the parent offtake, together about 8% of the cash cost. The domestic levy is the one policy that reaches a wholly domestic seller if the B50 funding need is met from domestic CPO; it is a bear risk, not a base assumption, because no domestic levy is in force in November 2026 [S10]. With the whole balance trapped at certainty instead of even odds this operating bear is worth Rp1,926, still above the current price: that is the governance-failure state, and it is quoted in section 5 rather than run as a fourth scenario because the bridge probability is a single model input shared by all scenarios.

bull.narrative: A severe El Nino and the B50 mandate lift CPO two fifths above the deck, as they did in the 2021-22 squeeze [S10, S11]: a 3m tonne loss of Indonesian supply in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68] meeting 14m tonnes of mandated biodiesel demand [S22, F69], a normal Q4, the maturing 6,054 ha of immature oil palm and a yield recovery from the weather-depressed base take volume 17.6% above the 300 kt plan; faster collection from SIMP releases working capital; and the extraction-rate and FFB-purchase programme hold the real cash cost about a quarter below the FY2025 level, the reciprocal of the bear's 30% cost stress [S3]. The announced Rp750bn buyback, running 26-Oct to 31-Dec-2026 on internal cash [S9], is carried as a probability-weighted partial in the valuation bridge, not as a scenario shock because its size is a ceiling. A step-up to the group sister's 50% payout is a board decision and is not added to the value: once the cash is credited at face, a higher payout distributes value already counted and is not an incremental asset; it matters only in the trapped state that the bear carries.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the 9M-2026 run-rate plus a normal Q4: CPO sales were 222 kt in the nine months (+7% yoy, [S3, F47]) and Q4-2025 was 82.5 kt of the 290 kt year [F1], giving about 300 kt. Production supports it: 9M-2026 CPO output rose 12% to 227 kt on nucleus FFB up 7% to 850 kt [S3], and FY2025 production was 292 kt [F33]. From FY2027E the plan carries the known maturity ramp: nucleus oil palm was 90,798 ha at 31-Dec-2025, of which 6,054 ha immature against 8,223 ha in 2021 [F32, F40], and the annual report states that an oil palm takes three to four years from field planting to commercial production [S6], so that block enters production over the forecast window. Mature area has fallen from 85,630 ha to 84,744 ha over the same five years [F40], so part of each year's maturation is absorbed by attrition, and the ramp carried is the net: 305 kt in FY2027E, 310 in FY2028E, 312 in FY2029E and 315 from FY2030E, about 5% above the 300 kt plan and 8.6% above FY2025 sales of 290 kt [F1], inside the 15% drift gate. That is below the gross arithmetic - the 6,054 ha at the FY2025 mature yield of about 3.4 tonnes of CPO per hectare is roughly 20 kt of eventual annual output, and 222 kt of nine-month sales already annualise to 304.5 kt [S3, F47, F32] - because the block matures over three to four years and the mature stock is shrinking. The 12-Nov-2026 GAPKI warning that El Nino could cost Indonesian production up to 3m tonnes with the heaviest impact in the 2027 harvest [S24, F68] is not cut into the plan: it is an industry aggregate on a national crop of about 60m tonnes, with no company or regional guidance attached [S24], and London Sumatra's nucleus output was up 12% in the nine months to September [S3]. A company-level cut on a national number would be the unsourced haircut the base-case rule forbids; the yield risk is carried in the bear at a 15% volume shortfall [S24], and the company sensitivity is disclosed in section 5.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated on the last actual, the 9M-2026 interim, and held flat. CPO (MKS) revenue of Rp3,342.357bn [S8, F48] over 222 kt of CPO sales [S3, F47] is Rp15.056m per tonne; at the model's FY2026E usd_idr of 17,570 [S0] that is USD 856.9/t against the deck's 9M-2026 average of USD 1,131/t (Q1 1,081, Q2 1,164, Q3 1,148, [S15]), a realisation of 0.758. The numerator and the denominator are on one series: the World Bank Pink Sheet states "October 2026: Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026" [S15, p.3], and the house deck records that "the World Bank re-based the palm oil series from January 2026 ... so pre-2026 annual averages and the 2026 monthly tape are not perfectly homogeneous" [fund record]. The audited FY2025 ratio of 0.852 (Rp14.114m/t against the pre-replacement 1,007 series at 16,448.09 [F3]) is therefore not the like-for-like comparator and is not used: no published factor bridges the old and new series, and applying a 2026-series ratio to a 2025-series benchmark is the mismatch the red team identified. What is homogeneous in rupiah is the realised price against the domestic Harga Referensi/KPB: Rp14.114m/t in FY2025 against the Rp14,234/kg KPB average [F41, S6], or 0.992. The 9M-2026 realised rupiah price of Rp15.056m/t is +6.7% on FY2025 while the new-series dollar benchmark is +12.3%, and the rupiah is +6.8% weaker, so the company takes the domestic reference rather than the export print; that domestic-reference lag and the unquantified series break together explain why the model carries 0.758 and not 0.852. Holding 0.758 flat rather than fading it is the last-actual rule; the peer ratios near 0.78 are measured against other benchmarks and are not directly comparable. At the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet rate of Rp17,998 [S8] the same revenue/volume is USD 836.5/t, a 0.740 ratio, which brackets the estimate from below. The mechanism behind the wedge is named, not assumed: (i) the export levy and duty, which move monthly with the reference price and were cut by a fifth to USD 246.36/t for November from USD 308.27 in October, a per-tonne charge on the exported benchmark that no domestic sale bears [S10, F38]; and (ii) the domestic reference itself, the Harga Referensi/KPB, which is administratively set and averaged Rp14,234/kg in FY2025 against the realised Rp14.114m/t, a 0.992 rupiah ratio [S6, F41]. Because the levy is a per-tonne wedge that falls as the reference price falls, a constant dollar ratio is the neutral middle between two defensible anchors: at the audited old-series 0.852 the engine target is about a tenth above the base but it re-imports the pre-2026 benchmark; at USD 856.9/t held flat in nominal dollar terms for ten years the realisation ratio fades with the rising deck and the target falls a mid-single-digit percentage below base, because the domestic reference does not follow the export print. Taking the middle and saying so is the most probable path; the flat-dollar world is carried in the bear's cost and price stress, not the base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no DMO-style domestic price cap applies to Indonesian CPO sales in this period; the B40/B50 mandate is a demand driver, not a cap on LSIP's selling price [S10].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Palm oil cost intensity is expressed per tonne of CPO, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a plantation [S7].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last audited year and escalated with IDR inflation only. FY2025 COGS of Rp3,250.368bn [F7] less the Rp373.058bn of depreciation inside it [F30] leaves Rp2,877.310bn of cash cost for all products; the non-CPO cost of Rp617.854bn on Rp1,418.588bn of PK, rubber and other revenue at the 56.45% other margin [F28] is stripped out, leaving Rp2,259.456bn of CPO cash cost, or Rp7.791m per tonne on 290 kt [F1]. That is 21% above FY2024's Rp6.420m [F31] because external FFB purchases jumped to Rp672.332bn from Rp488.924bn [S7]; we hold the FY2025 level rather than extrapolate either year. The 2.5% annual escalation is the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation [S0], so the real cost base is flat and the FY2025 gross-margin gain is not assumed to repeat.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar set to zero: the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS, so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S7].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling and port costs are already inside the per-tonne CPO cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [F30]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: 63.26% of revenue is sold domestically to SIMP [F34] and Indonesia's CPO export levy is borne by the exporter at shipment (USD 246.36/t, [F38]), not by LSIP on a domestic sale. The FY2025 cost-of-sales note carries no royalty or export-levy line [S7].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK, rubber, others)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-CPO revenue was Rp1,418.588bn: palm kernel and related products 1,093.304, rubber 149.982 and others 175.302 [F28]. It is escalated at 2.5% IDR inflation with flat volume, since PK output tracks CPO throughput and rubber prices move with the same cost base [S7, S0]; the FY2024 comparative of Rp921.664bn [F29] was lower because PK prices were weak, not because the product mix changed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 56.45%: the FY2025 residual implies Rp617.854bn of cost on Rp1,418.588bn of non-CPO revenue once the CPO cash cost is set at Rp7.791m per tonne [F28]. PK and rubber are by-products of FFB already harvested for CPO, so the incremental cost is pressing, handling and freight only; the ratio is held flat.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A of Rp389.453bn (fixed assets 383.284, right-of-use 5.129, deferred charges 1.040, [F13]) over the 300 kt plan is Rp1.298m per tonne. The pack's Rp4.8bn D&A line is defective and has been replaced by the audited Note 25 charge [F13]. The 9M-2026 charge of Rp304.770bn (segment 292.398 plus unallocated 12.372, [S8]) annualises to about Rp406bn, so the FY2025 base is not stale. Escalated at 2.5% IDR; there is no revaluation uplift because LSIP does not apply the PSAK 16 revaluation model [S6].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 additions to fixed assets were Rp433.312bn [F15], or 7.9% of revenue, spread across replanting, machinery, plasma and infrastructure (segment capex 393.856 plus unallocated 39.456, [S7]); over the 300 kt plan that is Rp1.444m per tonne. The 9M-2026 run-rate of Rp264.471bn [S8] supports the same intensity. Held in real terms with 2.5% IDR escalation rather than assuming a step-down after the current replanting push [S0]. It is not a low anchor: FY2025's 7.9% of revenue is the top of the four-year range, whose average is 6.8% (Rp320.7bn, Rp368.8bn, Rp376.2bn and Rp433.3bn in FY2022-FY2025 on rising revenue [S7, F15]). The annual report discloses no tree-age profile, replanting schedule or five-year capex average - the immature series [F40] is the only age evidence, falling from 8,223 ha in 2021 to 6,054 ha in 2025 [S6] - so a steady-state replanting stress at 10.5% of revenue is run as a bear cross-check in sections 3 and 5 rather than folded into the base: at that intensity the target is about 4% lower.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: LSIP's capex is volume-linked replanting, machinery and plasma support rather than discrete expansion projects, and the planted area has been flat-to-down (110,982 ha in 2025 vs 114,111 ha in 2021, [F32]); all of it is carried in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.3%, the FY2025 actual: operating working capital was Rp181.720bn or 3.3% of revenue in FY2025 [S0]. The FY2024 spike of 21.7% and FY2023's 7.3% [S0] are not extrapolated: the swing is the receivable from parent SIMP, 63.26% of revenue [F34], and the last actual is the right anchor. The working-capital caution is carried in the bear, which stretches the ratio 30%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 17.2%, the FY2025 effective rate: income tax of Rp391.187bn [F24] on pre-tax profit of Rp2,277.542bn [F9]. Held flat; the 22% headline is reduced by the permanent differences on plasma and land income that recur in the LK [S7].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8% on a negligible balance: FY2025 finance costs were Rp1.176bn [F23] against lease liabilities of under Rp1bn, and the group carries no bank borrowings at 30-Sep-2026 [F37]. The rate is set so a future lease or drawdown prices sensibly rather than at the engine's 15% clamp.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the three-year average of finance income over opening cash: 5.06% in FY2025 (Rp276.021bn [F21] on Rp5,453.691bn), 4.81% in FY2024 and 4.04% in FY2023 [S0]. The balance is held largely on deposit and partly at related-party Bank Ina Perdana, which supplied Rp44.005bn of FY2025 finance income [S7].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group has no interest-bearing bank debt at 30-Sep-2026, only lease liabilities [F37, S8], and capex plus the dividend are covered by operating cash flow of Rp3,015.733bn in FY2025 [S7]. The announced Rp750bn buyback [S9] is assumed to be funded from cash, not debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income or charge is disclosed beyond the associate line (a Rp5.691bn loss in FY2025) and that is immaterial against EBITDA [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: non-controlling interests are Rp3.833bn of a Rp13,999.946bn equity base and their share of profit was a Rp1.401bn loss in FY2025 [S7], so the minority line is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 30%: the company declares 30% of profit, DPS Rp83 for FY2025 and Rp65 for FY2024 on 6,819,963,965 shares [F18, S12]. The FY2025 cash payment of Rp443.234bn was the FY2024 dividend [F17]; the 30% policy is held rather than the engine's default.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: shares outstanding are 6,819,963,965 and unchanged across the audited years [F20]. The Rp750bn buyback announced in October 2026 [S9] is not yet executed and its size is a ceiling, so it is treated as upside in section 5 rather than modelled as a completed reduction.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal IDR, the macro deck's long-run inflation [S0]. With volume flat and CPO prices and costs both escalating at about inflation, real FCFF is flat; a 4% terminal rate would add real growth the business has not shown (nucleus FFB has been flat at 1.34-1.38m tonnes since 2021, [S6]).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (cash)
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the FY2025 net operating cost ratio: gross profit Rp2,261.338bn less operating profit Rp2,008.388bn = Rp252.950bn on Rp5,511.706bn of revenue [F11], net of other operating income (Rp136.905bn of FX, land-usage and PK-shell income) against selling Rp73.099bn, G&A Rp247.878bn and the Rp59.571bn bio-asset fair-value loss [S7]. It is not a cautious anchor: it is the lowest of the four audited years (5.8% FY2023, 6.1% FY2022, 9.7% FY2024 including the Rp296.164bn impairment [F12]), and the 9M-2026 interim does not lower it. The interim net operating cost is a credit of Rp70.4bn only because other operating income jumped to Rp290.800bn from Rp99.774bn - land-usage receipts Rp156.979bn against Rp38.318bn and net FX gains Rp125.908bn against Rp51.496bn [S8, F71, F72, F73] - and the biological-asset line swung to a Rp72.196bn gain from a Rp32.470bn loss [F77]. On the recurring lines the nine months cost selling 42.183 + G&A 220.090 + other opex 30.279 = Rp292.552bn [F74, F75, F76], 6.8% of 9M revenue of Rp4,326.692bn [F35], above the FY2025 ratio. Holding 4.6% therefore assumes the land and FX credits recur at their FY2025 rate and a normal, not a 9M-like, fourth quarter; at the interim's recurring 6.8% the target is about 3% lower. FY2024's 9.7% is not the run-rate because it carries the Rp296.164bn one-off impairment [F12].

challenges.challenge: The trapped-cash bridge rests on the premise that the related-party slice "never reaches minorities", yet the company's own interim shows the opposite direction of travel: the related-party balance fell from Rp1,639.556bn to Rp665.016bn in nine months, with the rupiah current account at Bank Ina Perdana down from 915.788 to 82.306 and third-party time deposits up 1,970 to 7,629 [S8, F39, F53, F55, F56, F57]. Cash still rose overall, so the Rp974.5bn was moved onto LSIP's own balance sheet at unrelated banks. The report applies a 58.9% haircut at a 50% persistence probability and asserts "no precedent" for a principal loss without disclosing the one movement that cuts against it.
challenges.answer: The Rp974.5bn outflow from the related bank is now disclosed in the valuation section: the Bank Ina rupiah balance fell 915.788 to 82.306 [F78], while third-party deposits rose 5,658.947 to 7,629.349 led by Danamon [F79, F80], so the money moved onto LSIP own balance sheet. The persistence probability falls from 0.5 to 0.35 and the target effect, under one per cent, is disclosed in the bridge [S8].

challenges.challenge: The base holds volume at 300 kt for ten years while 6,054 ha of immature oil palm - 7.1% of the 84,744 mature hectares - is maturing [F40, F32]. That is a sourced, known volume ramp, and it is credited only in the bull (+17.6% volume). The report justifies flat volume by "estate mature, planted area drifted down", which explains why total planted area is not growing but not why a known immature block adds nothing. Nine-month CPO sales of 222 kt already imply 304.5 kt annualised against the 300 kt plan [S3, F47].
challenges.answer: Base volume now carries the maturity ramp: 300 kt FY2026E rising to 315 kt by FY2030E as 6,054 ha of immature oil palm matures, with the annual report three-to-four-year planting-to-harvest horizon and the drift down in mature area giving a net maturation-minus-attrition path [S6, F32, F40]. Target effect about two per cent, disclosed in the investment summary.

challenges.challenge: The thesis is that the market misprices LSIP by 3x, but the report never marks the name against the entity that controls it. SIMP trades at 2.59x EV/EBITDA, 0.38x P/BV and a 4.8% dividend yield, and AALI at 3.28x and 0.76x [model.peers]. LSIP's own 1.27x FY2025 EV/EBITDA is therefore close to the group norm, not a standalone anomaly, and a minority in a controlled subsidiary cannot receive value that the parent's own minority does not. The report's peer cross-checks exclude both.
challenges.answer: SIMP and AALI are now explicit group anchors in the valuation section: SIMP trades at a lower EV/EBITDA and a fraction of book than LSIP, AALI at about three quarters of book; valuing LSIP at the parent EV/EBITDA gives about half our target, at the parent book about half the price. They sit outside the median on purpose and the DCF keeps its sixty per cent weight, because a controlled-subsidiary minority does not receive a mark the parent own minority does not [model.peers].

challenges.challenge: The GAPKI warning is treated as neutral for the base because it is national, and the nine-month output recovery is cited as the reason [S3, F47]. But the nine months to September 2026 precede the 2027 harvest the warning concerns - S24 dates the heaviest impact to 2027 and says the effect "mulai dirasakan pelaku industri" - so the 9M number is not evidence about the shock. No company guidance or regional exposure is cited, and the report's claim that "the deck's premium embeds" the shock is not attributed to any deck variable.
challenges.answer: The deck-premium claim is gone: the industry section now states the house deck is a CPO series with no weather variable, used at its published levels, and makes no claim that it prices the weather [S0]. The nine-month recovery is labelled as evidence about 2026, not the 2027 harvest the GAPKI warning concerns [S24, S3, S8]; company-level shortfall sizing sits in the investment-risks section.

challenges.challenge: Capex is held at the FY2025 actual - Rp433.312bn, 7.9% of revenue, Rp1.444m/t, about Rp3.9m per planted hectare - for ten years, from a tree stock the report itself calls old with only 7% immature [F32, F40, F15]. A mature Indonesian estate normally carries a materially higher immature share to sustain yields, so flat 300 kt output for a decade assumes the existing trees keep producing without a replanting catch-up. No age profile, replanting schedule or five-year capex average is shown, and the DCF has no reserve-life analogue to cap it.
challenges.answer: Capex disclosure fixed: the annual report gives no tree-age profile, replanting schedule or five-year capex average, and capex sits at the top of its four-year range; a steady-state replanting rate of about a tenth of revenue is run as a cross-check taking about five per cent off the target, leaving the rating unchanged [S6, F40].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E cannot be rebuilt from the 9M actual. The model implies Q4 revenue of Rp1,662.2bn and Q4 net profit of Rp445.7bn - a 26.8% net margin against 40.3% for the nine months - while Q4 gross margin is 47.2% versus 41.3% [S8]. The arithmetic driver is opex_pct of 4.6% (Rp275.5bn for the year) against a 9M2026 net operating cost of -Rp70.4bn (selling 42.183 + G&A 220.090 + other opex 30.279 - other operating income 290.800 - bio-asset gain 72.196). The report calls Q4 "normal" and never shows the build.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is now reconciled line by line to the interim in the financial section: the fourth quarter is normal, and the gap to the nine-month run-rate is the two non-recurring credits in other operating income and the bio-asset line [S8, F71, F72, F73, F77, F84]. Opex is held at the audited through-cycle ratio, disclosed as the lowest of the four audited years rather than a cautious anchor, with the interim recurring-lines effect, about three per cent lower target, disclosed [S7, S8, F74, F75, F76].

challenges.challenge: The investment summary uses "nine-month profit rose two fifths" as evidence the estate is improving, but 9M2026 other operating income jumped to Rp290.800bn from Rp99.774bn, of which land-usage receipts 156.979 (vs 38.318) and net FX gains 125.908 (vs 51.496) [S8 note 23]. That is 13.9% of 9M pre-tax profit and turns a roughly +28% underlying rise into the +40% headline. Neither the report nor the earnings-quality screen mentions it, and the model capitalises the FY2025 ratio instead, so the item is used neither as evidence nor as a risk.
challenges.answer: The summary now states the composition of other operating income (land-usage receipts and net FX gains [F72, F73]), labels it non-recurring, and uses the normalised underlying operating-profit growth of about a fifth instead of the headline two fifths. New facts F71 to F84 carry the interim composition, with F84 the prior-year bio-asset loss as its mirror [S8].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF says the price implies CPO at USD 640/t, 51.6% of the FY2027E deck. The report's own benchmark sensitivity gives Rp3,513/share at 0.8x the deck and Rp4,304 at 1.0x - a slope of about Rp3,954 per unit multiplier, which reaches the Rp1,560 price only near 0.30-0.36x. The offered reconciliation (the benchmark freeze "costs about a fifteenth") is far too small to bridge a 1.7x gap in the implied multiplier, and the freeze makes the grid's 0.8x cell more bearish than a clean 0.8x, which widens the gap.
challenges.answer: Reconciled: the sensitivity grid prints the blended twelve-month target while the reverse DCF solves the DCF leg alone. The valuation section now states that at a clean four fifths of the deck the DCF alone is about double the price, at half the deck about a tenth below, and the price is reached just over half the deck up, exactly the reverse-DCF answer of USD 647 against the deck [S0, S15]. The benchmark-freeze cost is quantified at about a fourteenth of the base target and about a tenth of the DCF.

challenges.challenge: The two multiple legs carry 40% of the target and both use contaminated peer medians. The 25-name EV/EBITDA median of 6.25x includes downstream refiners and holding companies at 10-46x (CBUT 11.35, MKTR 10.74, MGRO 28.75, NSSS 13.91, JARR 38.56, JAWA 46.22, FAPA 13.62) whose economics are not an upstream grower's; the 13 pure planters median about 5.1x. The 27-name P/BV median of 1.56x is lifted the same way (JARR 9.54, MGRO 6.53, FAPA 5.53, NSSS 5.23) against LSIP's own five-year average of 0.57x. The EV/EBITDA leg also applies a trailing FY2025A EBITDA of 2,397.8 to a 30-Sep balance sheet inside a 12-month-forward target.
challenges.answer: Both multiple legs now run on the thirteen pure upstream planters (AALI, ANJT, BWPT, DSNG, GZCO, PNGO, PSGO, SGRO, SMAR, SSMS, STAA, TAPG, TLDN) instead of the contaminated industry median; the EV/EBITDA leg is struck on the trailing restated FY2025A EBITDA, disclosed, with the forward-EBITDA effect of about one per cent and the unchanged 60/25/15 weights stated [S0, model]. Target effect about four per cent, in the investment summary.

challenges.challenge: The cost of capital is presented as measured but is not. Beta 0.80 is the PLANTATIONS config default - the assumptions state "no plantation name has a measured beta" - yet section 4 gives "beta 0.80 times the mature premium 4.2% plus country premium 2.5%, net of the 1.6% sovereign spread", which arithmetically gives 11.67%, not the 11.18% used. The engine's build multiplies the country premium by beta as well (rf + beta x (ERP + CRP) - default spread). The 1.62% default-spread deduction is also unexplained and lowers the hurdle for a name whose whole case is a governance discount.
challenges.answer: The cost-of-capital paragraph now gives the engine actual formula (ten-year yield less the sovereign default spread, plus beta times the mature and country premiums), discloses beta as the PLANTATIONS config default rather than a measured regression, and states the target at thirteen per cent, about a tenth lower, and at fifteen per cent, about a sixth lower and still about two and a half times the price [S18, S19, S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 asserts "The scenarios mirror the base shock for shock", but the cost driver is 1.30x in the bear and 0.80x in the bull, and the reciprocal of 1.30 is 0.769. The bear's cost stress is therefore about 10pp larger in magnitude than the bull's relief, and it alone carries the USD40/t domestic levy and the DSI pass-through with no mirror in the bull. Price, volume and working capital are correctly reciprocal; cost is not, and no qc_justification covers it (the orphan list addresses nwc_pct only).
challenges.answer: The cost shock is mirrored: the bear carries 1.30 and the bull now carries 0.769, the reciprocal, so neither tail holds a one-way cost stress; the scenarios section states the four drivers are reciprocal and the investment-risks section drops the old one-way language. QC justifications cover the mirror [S15, S0].

challenges.challenge: The update's own text says no model input moved, and the committed model is identical in every input and target to the working file, yet the summary says "the peer marks refreshed in the pack lifted the multiple legs to today's target". Either a peer refresh moved 40% of the target on market prices - which is procyclical for a cyclical and should be shown - or nothing moved and the sentence is wrong. Separately, the one-way stack (opex on FY2025, immature hectares only in the bull, payout at 30% while cash compounds to Rp27,922bn) is never quantified as a group.
challenges.answer: The false peer-refresh sentence is deleted: the committed model carries the identical peer medians and target, so no pack refresh moved the multiple legs, and the summary now says the peer marks are not one of the four changed inputs. The one-way stack is quantified as a group: the four changed inputs net to a target about one and a half per cent below the published one.

challenges.challenge: Two verifiable slips. The associate uplift "at attributable net assets ... about a twentieth of the target more" is 2.5% of the target on the report's own Rp804bn (Rp118 per share on Rp4,740), and the packet itself says "under a thirtieth". The catalyst date "2026-12-15" for the DSI palm export service fee is not in S25, which says only that the tariff will be announced in "Desember 2026".
challenges.answer: The associate fraction is corrected to about a fortieth of the target on attributable net assets, and the DSI tariff date now says December with no day, matching the source, with the catalyst frontmatter reworded to carry no typed numbers [S25].

missing_bull_case.note: Two absent positives. (1) The related-party cash fell from Rp1,639.556bn at FY2025 to Rp665.016bn at 30-Sep-2026 - the rupiah current account at Bank Ina Perdana dropped from 915.788 to 82.306 - while third-party time deposits rose 1,970 to 7,629 [S8, F39, F53, F55, F56, F57]. That Rp974.5bn movement out of the related bank and onto LSIP's own balance sheet is direct evidence against the "permanently undistributable" premise, and the report never mentions it. (2) The 6,054 ha of immature oil palm [F40] is a known, sourced volume ramp credited only in the bull; the base holds 300 kt for ten years.

missing_bear_case.note: The report never marks the name against its own controlling group. SIMP, the parent that sets the offtake, trades at 2.59x EV/EBITDA, 0.38x P/BV and a 4.8% yield, and AALI at 3.28x and 0.76x [model.peers]; LSIP's 1.27x FY2025 EV/EBITDA is therefore not an anomaly but the group norm, and a minority in a subsidiary cannot realise value the parent's own minority does not receive. Also absent: any replanting/age-profile stress (only 7% immature against 84,744 mature hectares) and any test of the 2027 harvest against company output rather than the nine months to September, which precedes it.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E does not reconcile to the 9M2026 actual: the model implies Q4 revenue of Rp1,662.2bn but Q4 net profit of only Rp445.7bn, a 26.8% net margin against 40.3% for the nine months and against a Q4 gross margin of 47.2% versus 41.3%. The cause is opex_pct of 4.6%, anchored on FY2025 (Rp252.950bn), while the 9M2026 net operating cost was a credit of Rp70.4bn. Volume, cost escalation and the zero-royalty treatment are otherwise well anchored and sourced.

evidence_and_citations.note: Most citations verify: F37 cash, F53 Bank Ina, F34 63.26% related-party revenue, F68 GAPKI, F58 buyback, F38 levy and the S15 p.3 "Replacement series for Palm oil from January 2026" all say what the report claims. But the 2026-12-15 DSI announcement date is not in S25 (which says only "Desember 2026"), the "a twentieth of the target" associate uplift is 2.5%, and the claim that the house deck "embeds a near-term El Nino premium" is an assertion about the deck with no deck source.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary, terminal growth and the cash/associate bridge are the right frame and the stub treatment is correct.
